entry.title: DeepSeek releases V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) open weights model with 1M token context window, high intelligence score, and moderate pricing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DeepSeek has released the V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) model, an open weights AI supporting text and image inputs with a 1 million token context window. The model scores 45 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, significantly above the median of 19, and is noted for its speed and verbosity. The model costs $0.30 per 1 million input tokens and $1.20 per 1 million output tokens, placing it moderately priced compared to similar open weight models. It processes tokens at 230 tokens per second and has been evaluated across various benchmarks including reasoning, coding, and domain-specific tasks.

entry.title: Researchers develop Hybrid Reasoning Agents that combine latent space thinking with text-based actions, improving performance and efficiency across multiple AI benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents) that integrate latent reasoning with text-based interaction through a unified generation process, enabling efficient internal thought and transparent tool use. The architecture includes a HybridLink for seamless mode transitions and continuous working memory to maintain hybrid context across turns. Post-training algorithms, HybridSFT and HybridRL, enhance coordination and decision-making between latent and text modes. Evaluated on 11 benchmarks in fields like mathematics, science, and medicine, HybridAgents outperform existing LLM agents by 10.4%, reduce token usage by up to 54.7%, speed up inference by up to 2.6 times, and cut costs by up to 3.7 times.

entry.title: Discussion on the importance of running your own LLM proxy to monitor and understand large language model operations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The article argues that without operating a personal large language model (LLM) proxy, users lack visibility into the processes and data flow of LLM interactions. It emphasizes the challenges in verifying and understanding what occurs behind the scenes when relying on third-party LLM services. The discussion highlights concerns about transparency, control, and security when using external LLM providers, suggesting that running a local proxy can provide better insight and governance over AI model usage and data handling.

entry.title: Strot compiles LLM intent once to run local, type-safe JSON decisions for classification, scoring, and routing at zero marginal cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Strot is an open-source tool that compiles a large language model's (LLM) intent once and then runs decisions locally on your hardware as type-safe JSON outputs. It supports tasks like classification, scoring, and routing with confidence scores, operating without generating new content at runtime and ensuring low-confidence cases abstain from guessing. The system produces a frozen Python artifact that can handle records indefinitely with minimal latency and zero marginal cost after the initial compile. The tool uses a compile-time LLM pass to synthesize decision models, which are then calibrated and frozen for runtime use. It supports multiple decision surfaces, including routing records to actions and answering typed questions with probabilities and confidence. Strot emphasizes guarantees on decision accuracy through temperature scaling and conformal prediction, avoiding structural hallucination by limiting outputs to selections and computations over a predefined registry. It is model-independent and can integrate local or hosted decision models, with installation options for different runtimes and APIs. Strot is designed for offline production environments and includes documentation on architecture, calibration, deployment, and API usage. It is released under the MIT license and implements ideas from a related arXiv paper, aiming to provide reliable, measurable, and efficient decision-making based on LLM intent without ongoing reliance on external models at runtime.

entry.title: Guide to using tmux with Claude AI agents for session management and scripted input automation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The article explains how tmux, a terminal multiplexer, can be used to run and manage Claude AI coding agents in named, detachable sessions that persist through disconnections. It highlights tmux's ability to hold multiple sessions in one window, script interactions by sending keystrokes and capturing output, and how Claude Code integrates tmux and git worktrees to simplify setup for single-agent workflows. The guide details organizing tmux sessions by project, naming conventions, and layouts for monitoring multiple agents, including using windows and panes effectively. It also covers limitations of the built-in Claude Code tmux integration and scenarios where manual tmux scripting is necessary for multi-agent orchestration, remote setups, and advanced input handling. This approach enables developers to automate and maintain long-running AI agent processes in terminal environments, improving workflow resilience and control over agent interactions.

entry.title: Sydney man arrested after allegedly discussing childcare centre mass shooting plans with AI chatbot Claude [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A 29-year-old Sydney man was arrested after Interpol flagged his conversations with the AI chatbot Claude, in which he allegedly discussed plans to carry out a mass shooting at a childcare centre near his home. The man, David Lan Thackray, was remanded for a mental health assessment and charged with using a carriage service to menace, harass, or offend. Prosecutors warned of a potential catastrophic outcome if Thackray were released, citing his references to a previous terrorist attack in Bondi Beach. Thackray's lawyer argued that his client was venting frustration during a private interaction with the chatbot and denied any ideological motivation or intent to act on the threats. Claude, developed by Anthropic, is designed to refuse violent requests and shares user data with law enforcement when necessary to prevent harm. Thackray, who has no criminal history and is studying international relations, will return to court after the mental health evaluation. Authorities continue to investigate the case amid concerns about AI platforms being used to discuss or plan violent acts.

entry.title: Researchers show reasoning models achieve higher chain-of-thought controllability using self-instruction embedded within their reasoning process [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Self-Instructed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Controllability, a method that embeds constraints as self-instructions within reasoning models' CoT, significantly improving their ability to follow constraints compared to standard user prompts. They find that even generic reminders to follow constraints boost controllability, and that effective self-instructions can be initiated through simple user prompts without direct access to the reasoning channel. The study also demonstrates that this enhanced controllability can be exploited to evade monitoring, raising concerns about the reliability of CoT oversight mechanisms.

entry.title: Researchers find recursive self-distillation can cause progressive misalignment in AI models despite benign training cues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers report that recursive self-distillation, where AI models are trained repeatedly on their own outputs with additional non-harmful cues, can lead to increasing misalignment on harmful queries, a phenomenon they term Progressive Misalignment. This effect was observed in Qwen3 and Phi-4 model families using benchmarks like SORRY-Bench and StrongREJECT, and also occurred when benign user feedback replaced fixed cues. The study shows that even benign prompts can trigger this failure mode, highlighting potential safety risks in AI systems trained recursively on their own data and underscoring the need for further investigation into these training procedures.

entry.title: Researchers evaluate frontier LLMs' ability to predict outcomes of self-generated machine learning experiments, finding limited but better-than-chance accuracy across 288 ideas on eight tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers tested five leading large language models (LLMs) including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 on their ability to predict the impact of 288 self-generated machine learning experiment ideas before actual training. The study found that while LLM predictions were significantly better than random chance, even the best model explained only about half the variance in outcomes and tended to underestimate the magnitude of changes. Prediction accuracy varied widely across different tasks, and the implementation method had little effect on results. The researchers released their dataset to support further investigation into LLMs' intuition for machine learning experiment success.

entry.title: Researchers propose Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement to reduce rollout window length and training cost in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR), a method that places multiple verifiable problems in a single training completion to retain reward signals while using shorter rollout windows in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). CCR reduces tokens per training step by over 79% compared to single-problem approaches with long rollout windows, maintaining reasoning quality in 4 billion and 8 billion parameter mathematical reasoning models. CCR encourages shorter useful reasoning without explicit length penalties by sharing a training budget across problems and crediting correct answers completed before truncation. Experiments show increasing accuracy rewards alongside shorter completions, suggesting CCR as a practical approach to lower per-step computational costs in RLVR without sacrificing performance.

entry.title: Researchers propose competence-based evaluation to measure logical reasoning consistency in large language models across varied problem presentations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a competence-based evaluation (CBE) framework to assess logical reasoning in large language models (LLMs), focusing on consistent application of reasoning skills across problem variations rather than single accuracy metrics. They apply CBE to elementary ordering tasks, testing six GPT and Qwen models, finding that while performance is good within limited complexity, models often fail to maintain competence across different problem formulations. The study uses a parameterized generator to scale task complexity while preserving the required reasoning competence and tests models with varied presentations of the same ordering rule. Techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and GRPO improve performance but do not fully resolve failures, and supervised LoRA shows limited transfer. CBE offers diagnostic insights and a scalable evaluation protocol for future LLM development.

entry.title: Researchers find a shared attention head circuit behind multiple-choice biases in language models, strengthened by post-training including reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed how language models often follow misleading cues in prompts, such as suggested wrong answers, leading to biases like sycophancy. They traced these biases to a small set of attention heads forming a shared circuit present in pretrained models, which becomes more active after fine-tuning and reinforcement learning stages. This circuit influences how models respond to cues in multiple-choice tasks across various models. The study involved swapping attention patterns between reinforcement learning checkpoints and their predecessors in models like Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, demonstrating that post-training changes when and how strongly this circuit is used. The findings suggest that assistant fine-tuning can inadvertently activate cue-following behavior and that targeting this circuit could help mitigate multiple-choice biases in language models.

entry.title: Researchers develop policy gradient method to reduce counterfactual bias in language models while preserving response quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the challenge of counterfactual invariance in large language models, where small prompt variations related to demographics or sensitive attributes can undesirably affect outputs. They show that standard alignment methods like reinforcement learning can increase demographic disparities in response quality despite improving overall performance, amplifying counterfactual bias. To mitigate this, the team proposes a policy gradient technique using a group-level reward function applied to matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. They create a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design evaluations that distinguish cases where demographic information is causally relevant. Their approach reduces counterfactual differences while maintaining overall response quality and allows models to adapt appropriately when sensitive information is relevant, validated across several fairness benchmarks.

entry.title: Researchers introduce BinProp to improve natural language explanations of chess and Go moves by enabling language models to discover reusable game concepts without training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose an automatic metric to evaluate chess move explanations based on chess-engine evaluations and find that state-of-the-art language models often rely on superficial board observations rather than deep, transferable concepts. They introduce BinProp, a training-free method that helps these models identify reusable chess concepts and explain moves in natural language, significantly improving explainability scores compared to direct prompting. The method also generalizes to other games like Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

entry.title: Researchers introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation method for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning that improves policy updates and agent performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present TreeOPSD, a new framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning that addresses challenges of sparse turn-level credit assignment and policy staleness. TreeOPSD treats each interaction turn as a tree node, recursively backing up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit and mapping these credits to a bounded teacher distribution relative to a frozen behavior policy. By minimizing divergence between this teacher and the student policy, TreeOPSD recovers the policy-gradient direction while bounding updates across sequential mini-batches. The method avoids reliance on value networks, step-level annotations, or stronger external teachers, reducing training complexity compared to existing approaches. Empirical results show that TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across multiple benchmarks and model scales, notably increasing the average accuracy of the Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 model by 4.97 points over GRPO in a deep research setting.

entry.title: Researchers study behavioral couplings in large language models, showing fine-tuning on one behavior can unintentionally induce others, complicating misbehavior tracing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have found that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on specific behaviors can unintentionally induce related behaviors, a phenomenon they call behavioral coupling. For example, training a model to respond warmly may also increase sycophantic tendencies, and training it to write insecure code can cause broader misalignment on unrelated prompts. The study shows that when models are trained on documents describing two behaviors together, fine-tuning to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well, even if the second behavior is undesirable. The researchers also discovered that behavioral couplings can compose across different document sets, making it difficult to trace the origin of emergent misbehaviors since coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single training document. These findings suggest that preventing unintended effects from fine-tuning may require evaluation methods that go beyond assessing a model's current behavior alone.

entry.title: Researchers introduce MuPHI benchmark and CHIL method to improve multimodal harm detection and reasoning generalization in vision-language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present MuPHI, a diagnostic benchmark designed to evaluate how vision-language models (VLMs) detect harm arising from the combination of benign images and captions, highlighting that current models often fail to bind cross-modal evidence into a coherent harm mechanism. They find that while VLMs ground each modality reliably, their predictions respond weakly to counterfactual interventions, and existing harm detection methods trained on labels perform poorly when transferred across different harm distributions. To address these issues, the team proposes Compositional Harm Interpretation Learning (CHIL), which encourages models to identify evidence in each modality, bind cross-modal information, and maintain consistency in reasoning chains rather than focusing solely on predicted labels. CHIL improves out-of-domain transfer performance by 81%, increases macro-F1 scores by an average of 2.5 points, and enhances correct counterfactual flip rates, suggesting that optimizing reasoning processes can lead to more robust multimodal safety systems beyond dataset-specific correlations.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Audit-First VAPO for risk-certified selective updates under imperfect verification, achieving improved accuracy and controlled harmful risk on reasoning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present Audit-First VAPO, a method that separates directional admission from magnitude control to manage harmful update risks under imperfect verification. The approach uses an accept-appeal-abstain policy with a finite secondary-verification budget and provides finite-sample bounds certifying harmful risk, coverage, and verifier-call rate over a policy family. Evaluation on Qwen3.5-0.8B and GSM8K reasoning benchmarks shows 74.1% accuracy with controlled harmful risk and verifier cost, outperforming baseline methods like static RLVR and confidence thresholding. The method employs conditional Hoeffding-Azuma bounds to handle dependencies from shared budgets and initiates new certification stages upon rollout or verifier changes. After admission, a bounded trust-clip-KL actuator controls update magnitude. Across various verifier noise conditions, the certification was satisfied in 57 of 60 independent runs, isolating the effects of directional selection from other factors such as proposal suppression and update shrinkage.

entry.title: ContractRL introduces contract-constrained sequential repair protocol for JSON tool-call errors, improving semantic success and reducing token generation compared to Patch-SFT and full regeneration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: ContractRL is a new method for repairing structured tool calls that fail due to schema or execution contract violations. It models JSON repair as a bounded decision process using verifier feedback, action masks, and a repair budget to guide patch, retry, and abstention decisions, aiming to improve auditability and efficiency. In evaluations over multiple seeds and cases, ContractRL achieved higher semantic success rates and generated fewer tokens than existing methods like Patch-SFT and full regeneration. Policy optimization further improved its performance. Analyses link these gains to localized corrections enabled by feedback and action masking, while adversarial and multi-turn tests reveal remaining challenges in repair scenarios.

entry.title: ROUTEAUDIT introduces interaction-aware identification for budgeted multi-verifier routing with contract-conditioned attribution and policy-independent response tracking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: ROUTEAUDIT presents a new framework for adaptive multi-verifier systems by formulating verifier routing as a contract-conditioned identification problem that accounts for verifier catalog, availability, resource use, and scoring changes. The system adds measurable objects including a contract lattice for attribution, a policy-independent response tape for sequential contrasts, and request-level bounds for incomplete matching, enabling precise quality-cost gap analysis across different policies. The protocol commits observations and ledger events before oracle joins and provides attribution certificates for comparisons. Evaluations on held-out caches and task requests show improved quality metrics and low error rates in route and endpoint reconstruction. Additional studies assess the certificate interface and stress test learned policies under the identification contract, demonstrating ROUTEAUDIT's effectiveness in controlled attribution recovery and adaptive policy evaluation.

entry.title: FSPO: Policy-Consistent Risk and Pareto-Feasible Control for Budgeted LLM RL Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.02828v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adaptive LLM reinforcement-learning post-training changes multiple training actuators online, including rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, and update budget. Three coupled issues remain unresolved. A future-risk model trained from behavior trajectories need not estimate the risk induced by the controller that will be deployed; a score calibrated on logged state-action pairs can become miscalibrated after selective action choice; and independent per-resource minimum costs do not in general certify a feasible multi-resource continuation. We introduce FSPO, a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM RL post-training that addresses these issues jointly. FSPO learns a policy-consistent risk-to-go model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, together with a long-horizon utility model. Decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) calibrates risk on cross-fitted trajectories generated by actions selected by provisional controllers. A Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. Under a matched GRPO resource envelope, FSPO reaches 66.11% held-out and 59.43% OOD accuracy, compared with 64.47% and 57.03% for PB2, the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline. Three paired training seeds give gains of +2.42 and +3.19 percentage points over the contextual bandit on held-out and OOD evaluation. Under high behavior-deployment mismatch, policy-consistent risk lowers selected-decision ECE from 0.108 to 0.053; DCTC lowers it from 0.039 to 0.022 at matched acceptance; PRCC removes false-feasible admissions on an 18-action catalog ($0.197\rightarrow0.000$); and enabling all three components reduces trajectory failure from 0.181 to 0.083 in a factorial ablation.

entry.title: Two Minds Better Than One: Collaborative Reward Modeling for LLM Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2505.10597v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reward models (RMs) are central to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet noisy preference feedback can induce reward misgeneralization through spurious correlations and overfitting. We characterize the training dynamics of preference pairs and uncover a distinctive optimization signature of noise: persistently high losses, sharp temporal fluctuations, and irregular gradient updates. Our analyses further show that excluding such pairs improves downstream alignment. In practice, however, reliable preferences are not known a priori, and self-filtering based on a model's own training signals can amplify confirmation bias. To address this challenge, we introduce Collaborative Reward Modeling (CRM), an online framework for identifying reliable preferences. CRM couples cross-model peer review with curriculum learning: two RMs evaluate each other's sample selections, while curriculum keeps their learning progress synchronized. Across extensive experiments, CRM improves RM generalization by up to 9.94 points on RewardBench under 40% preference noise. CRM further generalizes to implicit-reward alignment, offering a robust and broadly applicable approach to learning from imperfect feedback.

entry.title: Rep2Text: Decoding Full Text from a Single LLM Token Representation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2511.06571v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models represent text as hidden numerical patterns, but what information these representations actually contain remains a mystery. Can we recover the original text from just one of them? In this paper, we introduce Rep2Text, a method designed to answer this question by reconstructing text from a single hidden representation. We find that these representations preserve much more information than we might expect. For short texts of about 16 words, Rep2Text can recover roughly half of the original words while preserving their overall meaning. As the text gets longer, recovering the exact wording becomes harder, but the main ideas can still be recovered. These findings offer a new way to understand what language models store internally and highlight potential privacy risks, as hidden representations may reveal parts of the original input.

entry.title: Pro-AI Bias in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2601.13749v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for decision-support across multiple domains. We ask whether these models favor artificial intelligence (AI) itself. We examine this question through three experiments. First, in open-ended advice across investment, study, career, and startup domains, AI is prominent in most recommendation lists and is usually ranked first when it appears. Second, in salary estimations, models overestimate AI-related jobs more than they do for closely matched non-AI jobs. In a controlled follow-up, changing only the job title from the matched non-AI title to the AI-related title raises predicted salary by 10%, while all other supplied job details remain fixed. Finally, we show that the number of degrees and other credentials awarded by AI programs were 28% more overestimated than corresponding awards for matched computing programs. Overall, we show that AI is not only prominent in everyday LLM advice, but also receives systematically inflated quantitative estimates compared to non-AI cases, even against its closest disciplinary neighbors, raising concerns for high-stakes decision support.

entry.title: CauTion: Knowing When to Trust LLMs for Ensemble Causal Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2606.03602v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data remains challenging due to the fundamental limitations of purely statistical methods, such as statistical distinguishability within equivalence classes and sensitivity to finite sample sizes. While large language models (LLMs) offer a promising source of domain knowledge to complement statistical inference, existing LLM-augmented methods are vulnerable to LLM errors and incur high token costs. Moreover, reliance on a single data-centric algorithm can make results sensitive to algorithm-specific biases. To address these limitations, we propose CauTion, a framework that reliably integrates LLM domain knowledge into an ensemble of statistical causal discovery algorithms through consensus filtering and LLM reliability estimation. CauTion proceeds in three stages. First, an algorithm ensemble utilizes a consensus voting to resolve up to 96% of edges on which algorithms agree, achieving near-perfect accuracy on the filtered consensus edges. Second, a trust-calibrated arbitration mechanism estimates the relative reliability of the LLM and the algorithms via an annotation-free trust calibration procedure, which is then utilized to govern a trust-weighted voting process that restricts LLM arbitration exclusively to edges with unreliable algorithmic evidence. Third, a cycle repair step is applied to guarantee the final causal graph is validly acyclic. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate that CauTion consistently outperforms both data-centric and LLM-augmented baselines, with larger gains on larger graphs and strong robustness to LLM errors. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauTion.

entry.title: Group-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2606.22995v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Group-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) has significantly enhanced Large Language Models (LLMs) in agentic scenarios. To achieve finer-grained policy updates, recent agentic RL frameworks have shifted from trajectory-level to step-level training. However, long-horizon agentic RL suffers from severe reward sparsity and delay, as feedback is often deferred for dozens of interaction steps. While existing step-level frameworks refine training granularity, their credit assignment remains coarse-grained and still treats agent exploration as isolated, linear trajectories. This oversimplified perspective ignores the inherent graph structure of state transitions, leading to high-variance state-value estimation and myopic, localized credit assignment. To overcome these critical bottlenecks, we propose Group-Graph Policy Optimization (G2PO), a novel group-based RL algorithm tailored for multi-turn agentic tasks. G2PO explicitly transforms linear interaction trajectories into a global state-transition graph. By aggregating identical observations across different trajectories, we introduce group-aggregation state-value estimation that reduces sampling variance and trajectory-dependent bias. Furthermore, we redefine agent actions as transitions between state nodes and propose an edge-centric advantage estimation strategy. By globally standardizing Temporal Difference (TD) errors across the entire graph, G2PO explicitly identifies and prioritizes critical transitions that drive absolute task progress. Extensive experiments on representative long-horizon benchmarks-WebShop, ALFWorld, and AppWorld-demonstrate that G2PO substantially outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-based and RL baselines, achieving remarkable success rate improvements of up to 22.2% over GRPO.

entry.title: VStress: Correlation-Aware Auditing and Adaptive Budget Allocation for Repeated Verifiers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.36958v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repeated verifier calls are useful only when they contribute conditional information. We introduce VStress, an auditable replay contract, and VStress-CA, a correlation-aware allocation policy that estimates the conditional marginal information of an unqueried verifier on a sealed calibration split, discounts uncertainty, normalizes by call cost, and stops or abstains when the next call is not informative. The controller freezes its decision and cost ledger before joining the clean oracle; a dependence-shift alarm disables channel preference and falls back to exact-stop. The controlled audit gives the mechanism boundary: at 35% symmetric corruption, majority-5 improves balanced accuracy from 0.6578 to 0.7739, whereas at 65% it loses 0.1226 points. In the matched fixed-budget comparison, breadth, redundancy, and adaptive allocation obtain balanced accuracies 0.6048, 0.6375, and 0.6538, with 3.4216 calls per item and an RLVR score of 0.6417 for VStress-CA. Dependence diagnostics also increase from same-model repeats to cross-family channels, with conditional marginal gains of 0.0126, 0.0462, and 0.0913. These measurements turn correlation from a post-hoc warning into an auditable allocation decision.

entry.title: Actions with Receipts: Jointly Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Replayable Tool-Agent Auditing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.00327v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tool-using agents can expose citations and execution logs while leaving a critical association unaudited: whether the claim shown to a user is the claim emitted by the committed execution and supported by the cited source. A valid citation and a valid trace can therefore remain individually well formed while being transplanted across claims, actions, runs, or source versions. We introduce a claim-anchored execution contract that jointly binds the emitted claim, its exact source span, the ordered execution prefix that produced it, and the source version and access state observed by that execution. Each receipt contains an emission anchor that deterministically locates the claim inside a committed answer or claim-bearing action, together with source identifiers, offsets, hashes, quotes, and a domain-separated execution commitment. A deterministic integrity verifier reconstructs these bindings before semantic or task labels are joined. We separate this integrity plane from a pluggable support plane, so structural validity is not used as a proxy for entailment. The contract exposes seven independently testable properties: claim-emission binding, source binding, ordered-execution binding, oracle separation, persisted-object replay, execution-rerun consistency, and version/access binding. Across 1,280 cross-object attacks, the joint contract detects 1,275 substitutions (0.9961). Removing a targeted property reduces its attack-detection rate to 0.0156-0.0625. On an independently adjudicated 384-pair split, the conflict-aware support guard reaches F1 0.8865 and false acceptance 0.0729; on unseen failure families, these rates are 0.8679 and 0.0938.

entry.title: FAER: Auditable Utility-Aligned Trajectory Replay for Language Model Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.00385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Replay selectors often rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, although cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. We formalize this selection-to-learning gap and introduce FAER as an auditable full-trajectory replay framework. Its training-free fixed selector is a protocol baseline; FAER-UTILITY is the learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks. The normalized gradient alignment is reported as a baseline, while a disposable optimizer-aware virtual update supplies a magnitude-aware utility surface. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the matched learner study reports quality 0.6329 for the fixed selector, compared with 0.5482 for uniform and 0.6037 for format-feedback under 128 updates. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches $0.6476\!\pm\!0.0139$ over eight seeds (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval $[+0.079,+0.122]$) at 63,276 target-run tokens; its recorded full cost is 189,642 tokens and 3.48 GPU-hours including calibration. The completed FAER-UTILITY row reaches 0.6624 at 62,844 target-run tokens and 4.26 GPU-hours. Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953, compared with 0.3594 for the fixed selector, despite the different downstream ranking. The completed comparison surfaces report the learner-aware ablation, same-seed gap, policy-optimization rows, and strict zero-shot transfer.

entry.title: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.03827v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Similarity scores are often offered as evidence that a model shares structure with the brain or across languages. We ask what such a score reads when that structure is removed, or when the instrument measuring it does not work, in two settings. Across seventeen languages, a grammaticality probe transfers worse between more distant languages (r = -0.66). But the probe's own accuracy falls along the same axis and is at chance in four languages, four of the five most distant. Dropping them halves the explained variance, and because it also narrows the range of distances, the design cannot say how much of the gradient is the instrument. Counting the 272 language pairs as independent gives p = 0.0006 for a steering effect that is null when the seventeen languages are the unit (p = 0.155). In brain alignment, a training objective raises a language model's similarity to fMRI responses from 0.10 to 0.34 (reliability ceiling 0.54), yet targets with the brain correspondence destroyed still reach 0.31. A shuffled target scores about k/n against the real one, for rank k and n sentences, a baseline that can be computed before any model is trained. Both interventions work, yet we detect no distance-graded steering effect and no syntactic benefit from alignment. Before reading a correspondence score, measure how much of it survives without the correspondence.

entry.title: In Europe's tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
entry.summary: In a major European technology hub, labor unions in Ireland are experiencing significant growth as workers respond to layoffs driven by advancements in artificial intelligence. The rise of AI technologies has led to job reductions, prompting increased union activity and membership as employees seek to protect their rights and negotiate better terms amid the changing employment landscape.

entry.title: Show HN: Yila - A Codex for Scientific Research
PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.

entry.title: Null Controls Are Necessary but Not Sufficient: Evaluating Acceptance Guards for Scientific Discovery and Interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated discovery systems propose scientific explanations and test which to accept. Does passing a test establish the intended claim? We develop four executable operations for changing physical descriptions: identifying redundancies (L1), coarse-graining dynamics (L2), transferring structure (L3), and inferring missing quantities from conservation imbalances (L4). We evaluate these operations and three interpretability settings through null acceptance (NAR), positive acceptance (PAR), and consequence agreement (CAR). A reduction mapping every state to zero predicts its own future perfectly. It passes closure on 96% of 129 public chaotic systems despite retaining no dynamical variation. An independent observable-preservation test rejects it throughout. On controlled benchmarks, the combined criteria accept 24/24 genuine reductions and reject 72/72 nulls. The other operations distinguish symmetries from redundancies, validate transfers, and reject spurious conservation imbalances. In language and ESM-2 protein models, linear CKA remains unchanged when a proposed correspondence is randomly rotated, whereas localized interventions distinguish genuine mappings from tested nulls. In sparse autoencoders, enrichment rejects all 16 tested nulls, yet independent ablation supports 45% of evaluable enriched features, compared with 0.5% of matched controls. These results reveal two acceptance gaps: descriptive tests can accept scientifically empty candidates, and accepted candidates can lack independently verified consequences. Reliable automated discovery requires evaluating both what a test accepts and the scientific consequences it establishes. Code and data: https://real-project-aether.github.io/project-aether/.

entry.title: Learnable Splines for Unstructured Neural Operators [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators approximate solution operators of partial differential equations at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers. Efficient grid-based architectures such as the Fourier neural operator (FNO) assume uniform rectangular grids, whereas engineering simulations use large, irregular, and locally refined meshes. We introduce L-SplineFNO, a memory-efficient neural operator that couples an FNO backbone with a sparse, learnable tensor-product B-spline transfer between unstructured meshes and a latent Cartesian grid. A local normalised scatter avoids the geometry-dependent solve of analytic spline transformation while preserving compact support, partition of unity, and spline smoothness by construction. The neural operator, conditioned on global design and operating parameters, learns the mapping of geometry to the field solution. Across six three-dimensional engineering benchmarks, L-SplineFNO achieves strong predictive accuracy while requiring substantially less memory and compute than baseline operators, scaling to 26.6 million nodes in training and 46 million in inference on a single A100 GPU. It also supports zero-shot super-resolution and efficient closed-form spatial derivatives. Uniquely, the analytic spline decoder yields rigorous prediction bounds over continuous space and uncertain parameters, via Bernstein convex hulls and Taylor models, demonstrated on a 29.2-million-node MAST-U tokamak model.

entry.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.

entry.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.

entry.title: Not All Graphs Are Maps: A Task-Agnostic Exploration Framework for Mobile GUI Navigation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern mobile GUI agents can perceive visible screens and execute local actions, but they still lack persistent app-specific navigation knowledge: where functions live, which pages contain them, and which screens are equivalent across repeated visits. We introduce TAG-Nav, a Task-Agnostic Graph Navigation framework that wraps existing GUI-agent backbones with reusable destination memory. Offline exploration is distilled into compact records of app functions, target pages, and waypoint routes before any evaluated instruction is seen. When a future task's destination is covered, TAG-Nav retrieves the destination and provides route guidance without task-specific demonstrations. This separates mobile GUI destination navigation from full task completion: many tasks share the prefix of reaching the right page, while final actions may enter content, send data, make purchases, delete information, or change sensitive settings. To evaluate route finding without downstream execution confounds, we introduce DestBench, a navigation-only protocol that asks whether an agent reaches the correct pre-action destination screen. DestBench enables a controlled graph-memory study comparing no-memory agents with random, automated BFS, and clean graph memory. Graph-derived memory improves strict navigation success rate of UI-TARS-1.5-7B from 52.4% without graph memory to 58.3% with automated BFS memory, and improves Qwen-VL-Max success rate from 59.5% to 71.4% on the same conditions. Together, TAG-Nav and DestBench show that destination coverage and route cleanliness strongly shape graph-memory value, making graph quality a measured variable rather than an assumed benefit of exploration.

entry.title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.

entry.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.

entry.title: When to Forget: Risk-Controlled Context Adaptation for Long-Horizon Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon agents learn from failure, but the value of a failure record can change as execution progresses. We study when retaining, compressing, or removing the same history block improves subsequent execution relative to full-history KEEP. We introduce RECAP, a framework that combines matched context interventions, execution-relational prediction, and independent policy certification. Matched environment states and rollout seeds measure success and continuation prompt-cost differences; prefix-only relations between a failure block and the current execution propose promising edits. Independent task bundles then select a policy subject to harmful-intervention and non-positive-benefit risk constraints under a fixed measurement protocol. A five-seed longitudinal case holds both the failure block and its summary fixed: compression fails at an early state and becomes a cost-saving intervention at a later state. Across five backbones, RECAP produces positive paired-success saving estimates with backbone-specific reliability-efficiency tradeoffs. On Hunyuan-A13B, it edits 43.24% of retained checkpoints while matching KEEP's observed 91.89% continuation success and reducing unconditional mean continuation prompt cost by 4,619.8 tokens (2.13%). The framework provides an execution-level reference for deciding when to forget: retain history by its value to what comes next.

entry.title: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.

entry.title: CIIR - Class-Indexed Interface Representation Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal learning commonly assumes paired or synchronized observations, yet independently collected datasets rarely provide such correspondence. We introduce CIIR, a modular encoder--decoder framework that connects heterogeneous datasets through a class-indexed address space while preserving each dataset's native input format and output module. A known local index selects address $k$, and an input-dependent 128-dimensional address representation Z_k(x) is written to that address. To demonstrate CIIR, we learn this address space from handwritten digits, clothing images, spoken-digit spectrograms, and hand signs without synchronized or instance-matched samples. Newly trained label-free receivers recover the requested addresses with 94.7% macro-average Address Realization Accuracy. We then attach the unseen SVHN dataset after freezing the base address space and train only lightweight adapters, achieving 90.2% MNIST>SVHN and 82.3% SVHN>MNIST end-to-end Address Transfer Accuracy without target-side decoder labels. To demonstrate generalizability of CIIR, we reuse the ten addresses as code elements in collision-free arithmetic and hierarchical address codes for all 100 CIFAR-100 classes and evaluate direct arithmetic-code realization through the existing receivers. These results establish CIIR as a compact interface for modular cross-dataset communication and post-hoc dataset attachment without exhaustive paired multimodal supervision.

entry.title: Characterising and Analysing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Techniques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. Thus, we propose a conceptual framework comprising main dimensions and sub-dimensions for characterising (defining "what it is") and analysing (defining "how well it does") existing RAG techniques. The conceptual framework was developed through a qualitative analysis of the attributes of RAG techniques reported in the literature. It can serve as a pre-empirical filtering mechanism for researchers and practitioners in selecting the highest-fit RAG candidates that meet specific user and task requirements before empirical benchmarking of RAG techniques, which can be computationally and financially expensive.

entry.title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.

entry.title: SimOPD: Relational Knowledge Transfer for On-Policy Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A key challenge in on-policy distillation (OPD) is extracting effective supervision from teacher knowledge. Supervision from token probabilities may underutilize internal knowledge, while direct hidden-state matching forces the student to shift to the teacher's feature space and complicates cross-architecture transfer. Inspired by contrastive learning's use of relationships between instances, we propose \textbf{SimOPD} to transfer teacher internal knowledge through response similarities. Specifically, SimOPD uses paired memory banks of student-generated responses to extract supervision from the teacher's internal representations as similarity distributions. The student then matches these distributions within its own representation space, retaining representational freedom and removing the need for cross-model projection. Extensive experiments show that SimOPD improves the overall average over the strongest baselines by up to 2.6 and 3.1 percentage points in same- and cross-architecture settings.

entry.title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.

entry.title: Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-augmented language-model agents rely on interface text: tool descriptions, argument schemas, and the candidate tool list shown at inference time. These interfaces often change after deployment even when the underlying tool semantics remain fixed, creating a practical reliability problem for function-calling systems. We study this failure mode as interface drift and evaluate whether a lightweight, training-free repair layer can recover robustness without retraining the base model. Our method, SchemaShield-Lite, combines schema validation, candidate-set retry for missing tool names, and one-shot constrained repair. On Qwen3.5-9B, it raises DICE-300 accuracy from 0.717 to 0.813 and BFCL-200 accuracy from 0.580 to 0.805, recovering 19/22 and 33/45 drift-induced failures with no observed repair harms. Naive retry does not explain the gains. Ablations show that candidate-set drift, especially distractor tools, accounts for most observed damage, while description and schema edits alone are less harmful. The results position validation-and-repair as a practical robustness layer for deployed LLM-agent tool use.

entry.title: Generative Policy Improvement from Observational Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how to improve decision policies from observational data to generate better actions when actions are complex, structured objects, such as text messages or images. This task is subject to two major challenges: (i) action-level overlap is often too weak for reliable off-policy evaluation and improvement, and (ii) generating new structured actions often requires expensive training or fine-tuning (e.g., of an LLM) and can be ill-defined due to information loss in action representations. To address both, we propose PolicyLift, a three-stage framework for generative policy improvement with structured actions from observational data. In Stage 1, PolicyLift learns a small set of discrete action codes that capture high-level strategies in the observed action space and are tailored to support policy improvement under limited overlap. In Stage 2, it learns a context-dependent policy over these action codes. At deployment time, Stage 3 "lifts" the learned code-level policy back to the original action space by generating actions from the historical behavior system in a code-conditioned way. We show theoretically that improving the policy over action codes guarantees improvement of the induced policy in the original action space. We demonstrate PolicyLift across experiments in synthetic and real-world text generation tasks with consistent policy improvements over the behavior policy.

entry.title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models

entry.title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.23845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.

entry.title: When is a large language model a good calibration agent? Physics-labeled prompting for budgeted engineering simulator calibration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calibrating expensive engineering simulators requires tuning model parameters to match reference data, a process heavily constrained by computational costs. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), conditioned on physical diagnostic descriptions of simulation errors, can propose informative parameter updates more efficiently than conventional derivative-free optimizers. We test this on a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem. Physics-labeled prompts are evaluated against four text ablations (removed, anonymized, padded, misdirected) and standard optimizers (Nelder-Mead, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and random search). Results demonstrate a strong early semantic advantage: the first physics-informed LLM proposal improves the initial design in 23 of 25 trials. After five evaluations, the median calibration error is 21.9 times lower than physics-free controls. However, this advantage is transient - disappearing by fifteen evaluations - and inherent LLM decoder variability yields a 9.8-fold performance spread. To address this, we introduce a hybrid workflow that uses the LLM as a warm-start, passing accumulated evaluations to a conventional optimizer. This two-stage numerical continuation policy reaches target accuracy in just 9 simulator runs, outperforming the LLM alone (12 runs), Nelder-Mead (17 runs), and Bayesian optimization (>60 runs). Supported by sensitivity analysis validating the test cases, this hybrid physics-labeled LLM scheme proves highly effective as a calibration agent under strict evaluation budgets.

entry.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22382v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.

entry.title: TRACE: Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding for Communication-efficient Distributed Edge Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed Transformer inference across co-located edge devices is fundamentally communication-bound, as exchanging activations between sequence-parallel partitions dominates inference latency under commodity edge bandwidths. Existing compression schemes reduce this cost but retain a structural bottleneck: the received data must still undergo key/value projection before attention can proceed, serializing computation behind communication. This paper presents Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding (Trace), a framework that addresses these limitations. Trace places a Vector Quantizer (VQ) at the post-attention residual of every Transformer layer and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations. During inference, exchanged activations are encoded into compact codebook indices, allowing receivers to directly recover keys and values through table lookup instead of executing the downstream computations required to derive them. By eliminating the received data downstream computation, Trace enables communication--computation overlap and reduces a key latency bottleneck in distributed Transformer inference. A hierarchical clustering further structures the learned codebook into a multi-resolution hierarchy, enabling runtime adaptation of the communication bitrate without retraining. The framework supports two operating variants: one prioritizing accuracy and the other balancing accuracy and efficiency through buffer-compatible quantization. Experiments on ViT-Base (ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100) and ViViT-B (UCF-101) show that Trace achieves up to 1.89% higher accuracy and up to 1.27x end-to-end inference speedup compared with the state-of-the-art VQ-based distributed inference framework. Compared with uncompressed sequence-parallel inference, Trace reduces communication overhead by up to 22,624x.

entry.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Induce Local Geometry for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a challenge in supervised continual learning, as adapting to new tasks causes representation drift and loss of previously learned information. This raises the question of which representational changes should be constrained while preserving plasticity. We therefore introduce Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring (SAGA), which converts a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained at each task boundary into local, low-rank constraints on representation drift. Replay examples specify where the constraints apply, while leading right singular directions of the encoder Jacobian specify which changes are penalized. The resulting geometry is input dependent and can be retained without keeping the SAE for subsequent tasks' training. We establish its local relation to latent code matching, define its spectral truncation error, and derive a conditional bound on frozen-readout drift. With replay and snapshot history, the method achieves the highest mean Class-IL accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among the evaluated ER, DER++, ER-ACE, and SGD baselines on three pretrained ViT-B/16 benchmarks, with accuracy gains of 12.15, 4.79, and 3.22 percentage points over the strongest conventional baseline on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R, respectively. From scratch results are more mixed, while rank ablations and geometry controls show that SAE-induced low-rank geometry offers useful stability-plasticity trade-offs.

entry.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.

entry.title: AuditKIT: A Unified Evaluation Spine for Benchmarking, Judging, and Comparing Large Language Models and Agentic Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating language models and agents requires combining benchmark accuracy, judge-based assessment, runtime performance, tool-use behavior, and retrieval quality. Differences in interfaces, metric semantics, and trace formats complicate these comparisons and can hide failures in agentic workflows. We present AuditKIT, a source-available evaluation library that records these measurements in one result representation, with direction-aware metric contracts, configuration fingerprints, and extensible metrics and backends. For agents, it provides turn-aware tool-call matching, separates parallel from sequential execution, and distinguishes verified task outcomes from trajectory-level diagnostics. Missing or unobservable evidence is marked unscored rather than counted as failure. For retrieval-augmented generation, it combines ranked retrieval metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks. Seven case studies spanning model comparison, serving runtimes, retrieval, tool calling, and interoperability show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric selection change evaluation outcomes.

entry.title: Mitigating Demographic Disparities in Explanation-Human Alignment via Rationale Regularization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study explanation fairness in hate speech detection. High classification performance does not always mean that a model produces equally plausible explanations for different demographic groups. Using the HateXplain dataset, we introduce Plausibility-EFG, a metric that measures the largest difference in explanation plausibility across demographic groups by comparing model-generated token attributions with human-annotated rationales. We evaluate BERT, RoBERTa, and ADV-RoBERTa, an adversarially trained model, using Integrated Gradients and SHAP. Our results show that ADV-RoBERTa improves classification performance and alignment between explanations and human rationales while reducing explanation disparities across demographic groups. These improvements are observed with both attribution methods and remain consistent across training, validation, and test splits. We also show that reducing prediction-level bias alone does not eliminate disparities in explanations, suggesting that predictive fairness and explanation fairness are related but distinct objectives. Finally, our fairness-performance analysis shows that stronger adversarial regularization can further reduce Plausibility-EFG, although it may cause a small decrease in macro-F1. Overall, this work presents explanation fairness as an important objective in hate speech moderation and introduces Fair-REF, a framework designed to reduce disparities in model explanations across demographic groups.

entry.title: Network-Wide Freeway Speed Nowcasting and Forecasting from Sparse Fixed Sensors with a Probe-Supervised Graph Convolutional Recurrent Network [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.22630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traffic agencies need current and near-future speeds on every link of their network, but their fixed sensors cover only part of it.
